en: You lied, saying that you were a fat man.
Algara turned his mouth,
Aram Neet Karagul
Screaming.
That's when Kongurbay,
Steel door gate,
If you notice that it is positive,
If you are sixty,
He is the youngest son of the chin
Near Konurbai
Six thousand Chinese, like a number,
Abydan's husband Konurbai.
near Kongurbay,
A necklace, a coral stone,
If you look at the fire place,
Mixed with the bloodline of Lung-tung.
A Chinese in a dark suit
The strong ones are in the osher.
Manchurian who threw stones
The clean ones are here.
Horse player, runner,
They wandered without a car
Soldier's runner,
The moon ruled the universe
Konurbai's rebellion.
Inside that fortress,
Beneath the golden pavilion,
In the imperial garden,
Kongurbai was lying
At the time appointed for his leisure.
A shrill cry rang out;
No other living soul dared approach.
One man stood there in anguish,
Calling Kongurbai by name.
When they heard Karagul's voice,
All the guards bent low,
And every messenger
Ran scattering in every direction.
When he heard the great uproar,
His snoring ceased;
Hero Kongurbai, the great Kalcha,
Opened his eyes wide as bowls.
When he wished to step outside,
And look upon the people's welfare,
At the gateway door,
At the opening where messengers passed,
By the towering watchtower,
At the foot of that tower,
The open field stretched broad,
And people thronged across the expanse.
When he looked upon them all,
There among the people stood Karagul—
Here was a most astonishing sight.
The reason it was astonishing:
He was covered in billowing dust,
All of his head and face
Were splattered with blood.
Even in sleep such a thing enters no dream;
That Karagul should come to this—
Had anyone ever heard of such a thing?
When he looked at Karagul,
He had no beard as before;
Algara had no tail.
He had a shadow but no living form;
His tulpar had no tail,
And his burning heart had become an ember.
"From his father, gray-wolf Manas,
I never suffered torment like this.
Instead of going off with the booty, you two,
Why have you come to me?
You have a shadow, but no countenance;
Were the two of you dragged along?
You yourself remain, but your beard is gone;
Were you pierced and left for dead?
Karagul, you have a tale to pour out;
My heart is torn with doubt.
You and Algara, Karagul,
Were closer than any living pair,
But your appearance is dreadful.
Where is the deep-dug trench?
Where is the army
Besieging this Beijing before us?
Karagul, may you burn and die,
Was it you, my elder, who would come
Having suffered and grieved,
Having lost every limb,
And was I the prince who would behold you?
Where is Red-Mist Mountain?
Where is the foe you fought in slaughter?
You have a sheath but no sword;
When I look over every side of you,
You bear the marks of coming from carnage.
You have a horse without a tail;
From what grievous calamity
Have you escaped, ill-fated man?
Is there a close road free of ambush?
Is there an army that came out to fight?
They have long been our enemies—
Has a foe come from the Burut?
When I see your state, Karagul,
May no human bear your appearance.
Your strength and bearing are gone;
You look like a man who has been struck down.
You have been thrown into confusion,
Living day and night as you pleased,
Eating the barren yearlings of the herd,
You smooth-tongued swine,
You have let yourself be defeated.
Your words come out faltering,
Your strength is gone, Karagul,
And your eyes look weary.
Your words come out crooked,
You have lost your former bearing,
And your eyes show the torment endured.
Another self stands in your eyes,
A stranger stands within your body.
Is there a road through the gray mist?
Deprived of your beard,
Karagul, have you come here wailing?
Did an army come from the Kyrgyz,
Raising a gray-white banner?
Was there a moon-crested standard?
Tell me, Karagul:
Was there an uproar splitting the sky?
Looking over every side of you,
You have the look of one escaped from slaughter.
Your composure has departed;
What words have you brought?
Did they draw bows until arrows fell like rain,
And shoot their strange bullets like hail?
Have you come out of that tumult?
From an outcry that deafened the ears,
Have you come out of that tumult?
You look as though you escaped a net
From which no living soul gets free.
You look as if you came from a road
Traveled without rest for six months.
You look as if you emerged from water
No scout could ever cross.
Without evasion, speak of your sheath.
Karagul, son of the Chinese,
Tell the truth and speak no lie.
If a foe has come from the Burut,
If an unhealable grievance threatens
Beijing of the Kakanchin,
I shall ready Algara and mount.
I shall ride out and slaughter them all,
Taking the army that goes with me,
Kill old Bakai,
And drive them to their own land.
I shall plunder their possessions,
And wreak destruction in this way.
If the enemy is from elsewhere,
I shall drive them to their land.
Karagul, willingly tell the truth.
If a people has come of its own accord,
If an overbearing lion has come,
He came to behold a terrible spectacle;
Without leaving so much as a hair,
The bastard shall die by my hand.
The great sorcerer guarding Beijing
Has bestowed mighty power.
Who has clashed with me
And returned to see his people?
When wrathfully I make ready,
Can anyone come and contend with me?
While the precious head
Of me, hero Kongurbai, remains,
Can anyone grapple with me and win?
While my noble head still stands,
You are foolish, Karagul;
Can any man force it to bow?
While your noble lord watches,
Can one who clashes remain alive?
When I command and exert my strength,
While your mountain-like Kalcha remains,
Can a mountain withstand me?
Do not hang your head, Karagul,
Like one who has suffered hell.
While your mountain-like Kalcha remains,
Can assembled enemies prevail?
They stood face to face,
Against the khagan of Chinmachin;
If they faced him and fought,
How could they battle me?
Do not pant so, Karagul;
These words of yours are foolish.
If someone stands confronting me,
If some living man presses in,
I shall fire my gun and draw my bow,
And fight him with a roar.
There is no boat on the black water;
While my precious head remains,
No one can strike the khagan.
There is no boat on the open water;
While I, the Kalcha, stand in wrath,
No one can face me.
To be robbed of your beard—
This is a calamity for a man.
You will not rest without telling your pain;
Calling him the son of Manas,
Why do you praise so highly
A wandering orphan?
A man grows drunk on fat;
While you lay sleeping in drunkenness,
He must have ridden over you.
The wretch's young hero,
Saying, “The fool has fallen into my hands,”
Did whatever he wished;
Your beard and moustache,
He tore out every hair.
Ah, Karagul, what shall I do?
The hollow behind Beijing
Was a road I myself had scouted.
His father, that fool Manas—
Have you heard the report?—
Was a slave who deceived six times.
In the marsh by the black water,
Facing toward the qibla,
The falcon Manas knelt down
And was making his devotions.
Driving Algara hard,
I stalked him from behind.
When his brow touched the ground,
Above the back of his waist,
That accursed blood-drinker,
I stabbed him with my spear.
The doomed man, with his left hand,
Seized the spear as he weakened;
The trick he worked upon the spear—
When he took hold and pulled,
My spear broke apart.
Riding a horse like Kartküröng,
Wearing a robe with a flowered collar,
Azhybai, son of the khan of the Argyn,
Below my breast,
With his fringed steel lance,
Struck without looking back.
At times I came to my senses,
At times I could not gather my wits;
As I reeled to and fro,
Before any time had passed,
All the forty companions,
Who rejoiced at the word “slaughter,”
With their gray-headed elder leading,
Shouted and leveled their spears.
From all the forty companions,
From the midst of that fire,
It was Algara's strength that saved me.
Algara beneath me
Carried me off and saved me,
Fleeing over hillock and hollow,
Galloping away and saving me.
From those who came I hear the tale:
The spear lodged in the bone
At the back of his waist;
